title: The Humble and Deadly Cigarette
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the cigarette as an object and its history: its origins in Spain as a cigarillo (small cigar) made from discarded cigar tobacco, spread through the Napoleonic and Crimean wars and World War One, the role of Philip Morris, James Bonsack's rolling machine and W. Duke, Sons and Company, and the marketing to women, movie stars and Black Americans (including Uptown menthols). They cover filters (cellulose acetate, tipping paper, the 1950 Winston filter, light cigarettes with perforations), additives and ammonia-puffed tobacco, early health warnings from the 1600s to the 1980s Surgeon General reports, secondhand smoke, the tobacco settlement, and declining smoking rates, plus a listener mail correction about Mendocino brewing and a short anecdote-filled conversation about smoking experiences.

segments.title: Opening banter and topic setup
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about a song cover and Brownsville Station, then introduce the episode on the cigarette itself, suggested by listener Julia.

segments.title: Cigarillo origins in Spain
segments.summary: The cigarette is traced to early sixteenth century Spain, where poorer people reused cigar stubs rolled in paper, creating the cigarillo.

segments.title: Basic facts about cigarettes
segments.summary: Standard cigarette length of about 84 millimeters, sold in packs of twenty, possibly matching matchbook count; cigarettes described as heated tobacco products.

segments.title: Nicotine and tobacco company research
segments.summary: Cigarettes deliver nicotine, which is addictive; tobacco company research later handed to state attorneys general. Additives list of 599 items released in 1994, with arsenic noted.

segments.title: Anatomy of a cigarette and filters
segments.summary: Describes paper wrap, adhesive, mainstream and sidestream smoke, cellulose acetate filters, charcoal claims, plug wrap and brown tipping paper treated to turn brown, and littered cigarette butts as photodegradable plastic.

segments.title: Spread of cigarillos through Europe and wars
segments.summary: Cigarillos spread slowly to Italy and Portugal in the late 1700s, then hitchhiked with soldiers; French and British soldiers during the Napoleonic and Crimean wars popularized cigarettes and the French term.

segments.title: Philip Morris and hand-rolled cigarettes
segments.summary: Philip Morris opened a Bond Street tobacconist shop in 1847 making cigarettes by hand; the hosts discuss the link to the modern company and the rise of machine-made American cigarettes.

segments.title: Duke and the rolling machine
segments.summary: James Duke's W. Duke, Sons and Company used James Bonsack's rolling machine, which made about 200 cigarettes a minute, cutting costs; early state laws on selling cigarettes to minors appeared in the 1890s.

segments.title: World War One and cigarette boom
segments.summary: Cigarettes spread to American troops in World War One, supplied by government and citizens; sales figures for Camel rose sharply through 1919.

segments.title: Cigarettes and women after World War One
segments.summary: Wartime changes loosened norms, women began smoking, and tobacco companies launched advertising aimed at women, including Marlboro's origin as a women's cigarette called Mild as May.

segments.title: Cigarette glamour, cases, and car lighters
segments.summary: Discussion of cigarette cases and glamour in old movies and books, plus cigarette lighters becoming standard in cars around 1925-1926.

segments.title: Hollywood cigarette endorsements
segments.summary: Movie stars received sponsorship deals with Lucky Strike and appeared smoking on screen; a push exists to rate movies for smoking content.

segments.title: Smoking everywhere and early health concerns
segments.summary: By mid-century cigarettes held 81 percent of the tobacco market and smoking was everywhere; Dr. John Hill's 1760s warning about snuff use is described.

segments.title: Early research and the Winston filter
segments.summary: Early tests linked tobacco extract to cancer; by 1950 studies linked smoking to lung cancer; the Winston of 1950 was the first mass-marketed filtered cigarette, largely a marketing ruse; smoking rates fell from 42 percent in 1965 to 11 percent in 2023.

segments.title: Light cigarettes and filter engineering
segments.summary: Tobacco companies spent heavily on filter design; light cigarettes differ mainly by tiny perforations in the tipping paper that let in outside air.

segments.title: Break and convenience store anecdotes
segments.summary: Ad break followed by hosts recalling working at convenience stores and cheap cigarette brands; the hosts mention cigarette sizes like Parliament and Camel Wide.

segments.title: Personal smoking anecdotes
segments.summary: Hosts share personal memories of smoking slim cigarettes, social smoking, and quitting difficulty.

segments.title: Puffed tobacco and ammonia
segments.summary: Companies used ammonia and freon to expand tobacco, getting more cigarettes from less tobacco; ammonia still used to increase nicotine absorption.

segments.title: Menthol cigarettes and targeting Black Americans
segments.summary: Menthol use among Black smokers, tobacco advertising in the Black press, and the 1990 Uptown cigarette launch that was withdrawn after protest led by Health and Human Services Secretary Louis Sullivan; menthol remains exempt from flavor bans.

segments.title: Surgeon General reports and secondhand smoke
segments.summary: Timeline of Surgeon General reports and warning labels from 1964 to the mid-1980s; discussion of secondhand smoke and smoking in cars and homes.

segments.title: Smoke-free public places and homes
segments.summary: Smoking bans spread to restaurants, bars, and flights; people began banning smoking in their homes.

segments.title: Quitting aids, tobacco settlement, and vaping
segments.summary: Nicotine patches and gum arrived in the early 1990s; the tobacco settlement is mentioned; teen vaping figures fell from 28 percent in 2019 to 10 percent three years later; cigarette sales rose even as smoker percentages fell.

segments.title: Global smoking and Vegas anecdote
segments.summary: Philip Morris revenue mentioned; smoking differences across countries; anecdotes about smoking in Japan and a Las Vegas casino dinner.

segments.title: Listener mail correction
segments.summary: Listener Devon corrects a Mendocino versus Adesto beer mix-up from an earlier USAID episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give the email address for listener mail.
